title: Geometric Primitives
content: The formalization represents points in ℝ² via Mathlib's EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2), with PointSet as Finset Point. The predicates InGeneralPosition (no three collinear) and IsConvexKGon (k vertices in convex position) are axiomatized since full definitions require cross-product and convex-hull infrastructure not needed for the combinatorial content of the problem.
mathContext: A point $p \in \mathbb{R}^2$ is represented as $p : \text{Fin}\,2 \to \mathbb{R}$. General position means for any three points $p_1, p_2, p_3$, the determinant $\det\begin{pmatrix} p_2 - p_1 & p_3 - p_1 \end{pmatrix} \neq 0$.

title: Empty Convex Polygons
content: An empty convex k-gon in a point set S is a convex k-gon whose interior contains no other points of S. This 'emptiness' condition is the key distinction from the Happy Ending Problem (#107): it makes the problem much harder and causes the function g(k) to have a finite threshold. IsEmptyConvexKGon is axiomatized with a structural axiom guaranteeing vertices lie in S.
mathContext: A convex $k$-gon $P$ with vertices $\{v_1, \ldots, v_k\} \subseteq S$ is \emph{empty} if $\text{int}(\text{conv}(v_1, \ldots, v_k)) \cap S = \emptyset$. The predicate $\text{ContainsEmptyKGon}(S, k)$ asserts $\exists V \subseteq S,\; |V| = k \land \text{IsEmptyConvexKGon}(S, V, k)$.

title: The Function g(k)
content: g(k) is defined as Option ℕ using Nat.find: it returns some n (the smallest threshold) when a finite threshold exists, and none otherwise. This elegant formulation captures both existence and non-existence in a single definition, enabling the characterization theorem g_exists_iff.
mathContext: $g(k) = \begin{cases} \min\{n : \forall S \text{ in general position},\; |S| \ge n \Rightarrow S \text{ contains an empty convex } k\text{-gon}\} & \text{if such } n \text{ exists} \\ \text{none} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$

title: Known Exact Values of g
content: Four axioms record the known values: g(3)=3 (trivial), g(4)=5 (Erdős), g(5)=10 (Harborth 1978), and g(6)=30 (Heule-Scheucher 2024). The g(6)=30 result was a landmark: existence was proved by Nicolás (2007) and Gerken (2008), but the exact value required SAT solvers verifying all 29-point configurations and finding a 30-point universal property.
mathContext: $g(3) = 3$, $g(4) = 5$, $g(5) = 10$, $g(6) = 30$. The sequence grows rapidly: the ratio $g(k)/g(k{-}1)$ is $5/3 \approx 1.67$, $10/5 = 2$, $30/10 = 3$, suggesting super-exponential growth within the finite range.

title: Horton's Theorem: g(7) Does Not Exist
content: Horton (1983) constructed arbitrarily large point sets in general position containing no empty 7-gon. The key idea: recursively interlace two smaller Horton sets so that any potential empty heptagon must use points from both halves, but the interlacing prevents this. The theorem g_7_not_exists is actually proved (not axiomatized) from the horton_sets_exist axiom, demonstrating a genuine deduction in the formalization.
mathContext: A Horton set $H_n$ of $n$ points satisfies $\text{InGeneralPosition}(H_n)$ and $\lnot\text{ContainsEmptyKGon}(H_n, 7)$. Since $H_n$ exists for all $n$, no threshold $g(7)$ can exist: for any candidate $n$, $H_n$ is a counterexample with $|H_n| = n$ points but no empty heptagon.

title: Bounds and Growth of g(k)
content: The lower bound g(k) ≥ 2k − 3 for 3 ≤ k ≤ 6 is axiomatized from known results. The theorem g_exists_le_6 is proved by case analysis on k ∈ {3,4,5,6}, dispatching each case via the known-value axioms. Lean's interval_cases tactic automates the case split.
mathContext: For $3 \le k \le 6$: $g(k) \ge 2k - 3$. This gives $g(3) \ge 3$, $g(4) \ge 5$, $g(5) \ge 7$, $g(6) \ge 9$. The actual values $3, 5, 10, 30$ exceed these bounds significantly for $k = 5, 6$.

title: The Horton Construction
content: The recursive Horton construction starts from a base point and builds larger sets by merging two Horton sets of equal size. The axiom horton_recursive guarantees closure under this merge. Crucially, horton_has_empty_6 records that Horton sets of ≥ 30 points do contain empty hexagons — the construction specifically avoids heptagons but permits smaller empty polygons.
mathContext: Given Horton sets $H_1, H_2$ with $|H_1| = |H_2|$, there exists $H$ with $|H| = |H_1| + |H_2|$ and $\text{IsHortonSet}(H)$. For $|H| \ge 30$: $\text{ContainsEmptyKGon}(H, 6) = \text{true}$, consistent with $g(6) = 30$.

title: Connection to the Happy Ending Problem
content: The Happy Ending Problem (Erdős #107) asks the same question without the emptiness condition. Its function g'(k) exists for ALL k (Erdős-Szekeres 1935), with conjectured value 2^(k-2)+1. The contrast is striking: removing the emptiness requirement eliminates the k=7 threshold entirely. The axiom empty_implies_nonempty formalizes g(k) ≥ g'(k), since every empty polygon is also a (non-empty) polygon.
mathContext: The Erdős-Szekeres theorem gives $g'(k) \le \binom{2k-4}{k-2} + 1$. The conjecture is $g'(k) = 2^{k-2} + 1$, verified for $k \le 6$. Since every empty convex $k$-gon is also a convex $k$-gon, $g(k) \ge g'(k)$ whenever both are defined.

title: Computational Verification of g(6) = 30
content: The determination of g(6) = 30 required both directions: a 29-point witness set in general position with no empty hexagon (lower bound), and a proof that every 30-point set in general position contains one (upper bound). The lower bound was found by exhaustive search; the upper bound was established by Heule and Scheucher (2024) using SAT solvers encoding the geometric constraints as propositional formulas.
mathContext: Lower bound: $\exists S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2,\; |S| = 29 \land \text{InGeneralPosition}(S) \land \lnot\text{ContainsEmptyKGon}(S, 6)$. Upper bound: $\forall S,\; |S| \ge 30 \land \text{InGeneralPosition}(S) \Rightarrow \text{ContainsEmptyKGon}(S, 6)$.
